added_claims.speaker: Ronald Reagan (clip)
added_claims.quote: high tariff legislation passed back in that period called the Smoot Holly tariff greatly deepened the depression and prevented economic recovery
added_claims.claim: The Smoot-Hawley tariff of the 1930s is the historical evidence that broad tariffs deepen downturns and delay recovery.
added_claims.direction: broad tariffs -> deeper depression, slower recovery
added_claims.conditions: Applies to broad, structural tariffs rather than narrow ones.

added_claims.speaker: Ronald Reagan (clip)
added_claims.quote: High tariffs inevitably lead to retaliation by foreign countries and the triggering of fierce trade wars.
added_claims.claim: Tariffs create a spiral: protected domestic firms stop innovating, foreign retaliation triggers trade wars, prices rise and demand falls, markets shrink and jobs are lost.
added_claims.direction: trade volumes, competition and employment fall
added_claims.conditions: Needs retaliation by trading partners.
added_claims.testable: partly - spiral is testable on past tariff episodes, not on this one

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: We're not adding up everything the right way. We're only looking at physical goods, their services, and intellectual property and net income that comes from um companies like Meta operating around the globe.
added_claims.claim: Goods-only trade deficit statistics omit services, intellectual property and the foreign earnings of US multinationals, so the headline imbalance used to justify tariffs overstates the problem (relaying Ricardo Hausmann).
added_claims.indicator: trade balance incl. services, IP and net foreign income
added_claims.conditions: Argument about measurement, not a trading signal.
added_claims.testable: yes - alternative trade-balance measures can be compared

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: they're nervous about the tenure. They're nervous about the impact on the dollar.
added_claims.claim: Tariff escalation puts the 10-year Treasury and the dollar under stress, which makes Congress, including Republicans who have historically opposed tariffs, push back and raises the chance of policy reversal.
added_claims.direction: yields up, dollar down on tariff escalation
added_claims.conditions: Cited as concern at the time, no data given.
added_claims.testable: partly - yields and dollar are observable but the causal link is asserted

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: national security must take priority over free trade and might make the argument I think that in particular creating resilience in these industries rare earths you know chip fabs in the United States
added_claims.claim: The realist (Mearsheimer, voiced by Sacks) counter-argument is that in a great-power struggle with a peer rival, national security outranks free trade, so domestic capacity in rare earths, chips, autos, steel and aluminum justifies protection.
added_claims.conditions: Steelman of the opposing side, not Gerstner's own view.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: he goes to the point of saying look we need to force them to do JVS here so we can learn from them.
added_claims.claim: Where China leads in advanced manufacturing, the US gains more by learning through joint ventures (as it did from Japan in just-in-time autos) than by shutting Chinese firms out.
added_claims.conditions: Depends on China being ahead in manufacturing technology.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: if you're using the word resilient, you know, that can include other countries that are allies.
added_claims.claim: Supply-chain resilience can be achieved by diversifying to allied countries, not only by reshoring to the US, so it does not by itself justify high tariffs.
added_claims.conditions: Works only if trade policy is consistent enough for firms to build the new supply chains.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: And I think that's uh he he used the word fanciful, which I would agree with.
added_claims.claim: Regretting global trade compares today's reality with an imaginary counterfactual in which the US kept its manufacturing and was better off; Niall Ferguson calls that fanciful.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: A lot of people think that what you know the historical telling is that what brought the wall down ultimately uh against Soviet Russia was that our economy was triumphant.
added_claims.claim: In the Cold War the US won by economic strength rather than by blockade, and targeted embargoes were reasonable; this supports an economy-first rather than a tariff-first approach to China.
added_claims.conditions: Historical analogy; targeted embargoes distinguished from broad tariffs.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: it's not clear out of the White House what the goal and objective is.
added_claims.claim: An unclear policy objective (tactical reshoring versus Navarro-scale tariffs) means broad bipartisan opposition if the larger version is intended, which adds to market uncertainty.
added_claims.conditions: Resolves if the administration commits to the narrow objective.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: the AI boom in the US has attracted more capital dollars than I've ever seen accumulated in the history of mankind.
added_claims.claim: Government subsidies add little where private capital is already abundant (AI), and public allocation invites picking winners and regulatory capture.
added_claims.conditions: Strongest for sectors already attracting abundant private capital.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: the private sector has done a more efficient job of uh, you know, of taking on the Manhattan uh, project, you know, style project.
added_claims.claim: Large Manhattan-style projects such as AI supercomputer clusters (Abilene and Denton, Texas) have been delivered more efficiently by private capital than by government in the past 40 to 50 years.
added_claims.conditions: Government role is needed where cost problems are regulatory, as in nuclear.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: Trump has said that, you know, he doesn't expect uh the the tariffs to stay anywhere close to where they are in China.
added_claims.claim: A presidential signal that China tariffs will be unilaterally walked down from the 140% peak is treated as an off-ramp from the escalation.
added_claims.conditions: Contingent on reciprocal moves by China on the rare earth ban.
added_claims.testable: partly - event can be checked, effect on markets is a single episode

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: The H20 was a nerfed chip, right? It was a chip that was two or three generations behind what we have in this country.
added_claims.claim: The banned H20 was a deliberately downgraded chip two or three generations behind US products, so banning it gave little security benefit while costing sales.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: you designed this product specifically to meet the expert control rule that was in place before this one
added_claims.claim: A company that complies with one export-control rule can be hit by the next, as with Nvidia's H20 and with firms that moved from China to Vietnam, so government rule changes are an uncontrollable single-stock risk.
added_claims.conditions: Applies to firms with large exposure to politically sensitive markets.
added_claims.testable: partly - event study of policy shocks is possible

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: Now they start working with this and they all collectively help improve it over time
added_claims.claim: Cutting Nvidia out of China makes every Chinese AI firm build on Huawei, creating an isolated ecosystem that improves collectively and erodes Nvidia's CUDA lock-in.
added_claims.direction: Huawei stack improves; Nvidia loses China share
added_claims.conditions: Needs Huawei to be near the frontier.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: I don't think we should be sending GB200s or cutting edge chips to China.
added_claims.claim: Gerstner separates frontier chips (restrict) from the older H20 (allow): selling H20 kept Chinese firms on CUDA and denied Huawei monopoly profits, so banning it was self-defeating.
added_claims.conditions: He calls it a close call, not a firm view.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: maybe 30 or 40% of all their sales were going into China
added_claims.claim: Reports that 30 to 40% of Nvidia sales went to China show how concentrated the revenue exposure to export-control risk is.
added_claims.conditions: Rumour-level number; Gerstner relays it as insinuation.
added_claims.testable: yes - revenue disclosures can check it

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: you get the exact opposite outcome from which the policy intended to create.
added_claims.claim: Complex policy often fails and sometimes backfires even inside the US; export controls are external regulation over a world where the US controls few pieces, so the failure risk is higher.
added_claims.conditions: Strongest when the controlled good is widely sold and has digital attributes.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: so you you mean global expert controls didn't work, so we're going to redouble them and see if they work again.
added_claims.claim: Proponents argue that previous (Biden) chip rules failed and therefore need tightening; this is circular, because controls that leaked before will leak again.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: But we just talked about there are 100 nuclear power plants under construction in China. Power is not their limit.
added_claims.claim: Huawei can offset weaker chips with two to three times as many chips and power; China is building about 100 nuclear plants at a quarter of US cost, so if AI is power-limited China is advantaged.
added_claims.indicator: Chinese nuclear build-out; chip count and power per unit of compute
added_claims.direction: China AI capacity up relative to US
added_claims.conditions: Holds if AI scaling is power-constrained.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: Nvidia just had a big announcement, right, with the White House about a $500 billion investment, right, in combination with a bunch of other comp companies, Foxcon, TSMC, etc. building fabs in the United States.
added_claims.claim: Private commitments (Nvidia's $500B US investment with Foxconn and TSMC, first GB200 off the Arizona line) show reshoring can happen through incentives without broad tariffs.
added_claims.conditions: Announcements, not yet delivered.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: There's there's a lot of arguments that the AI gap has been shrinking, not not rising.
added_claims.claim: The US lead in AI is shrinking (Eric Schmidt, SemiAnalysis on Huawei), so a strategy built on widening the gap is unrealistic.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: interdependence is no longer our choice it's our condition our only choice is whether we forge healthy interdependencies and rise together or maintain healthy interdependencies and fall together
added_claims.claim: Global economic interdependence is a given, so policy should shape healthy interdependence rather than try to cut it (Thomas Friedman quote relayed by Gurley).

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: the obsession and the time spent and the distraction for US CEOs to try to how to how they comply with all of this um I think is not particularly great.
added_claims.claim: Export-control churn imposes a compliance and attention cost on US executives that diverts effort from building.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: the thought that they couldn't, you know, be educated or can't innovate is going to lead you to a lot of really bad policies.
added_claims.claim: Assuming China cannot innovate leads to bad policy, because Chinese engineers are trained in the same universities and, as even hawks agree, China will have a frontier compute stack and frontier models whether or not the US helps.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: We are effectively taxing the Chinese on a nerfed product to provide profits to Nvidia to further distance the lead uh you know against Huawei
added_claims.claim: Roughly $15B of H20 sales yields $8-9B of Nvidia earnings and $2-3B of US corporate tax, so banning the sale gives up profit that funded Nvidia's lead and Treasury revenue while Huawei's chips already exceed the H20.
added_claims.indicator: H20 sales ($15B), Nvidia earnings, US corporate tax
added_claims.conditions: Arithmetic is Gerstner's own estimate.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: I'm going to deprive you of being able to build your national security or your national economic security, right? Like, it's it's a serious it's a serious thing.
added_claims.claim: If AI is treated as existential to national security, blocking a rival's access to it is an aggressive act and invites escalation.
added_claims.conditions: Depends on AI being seen as strategic by the rival.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: whoever got to space first was going to have this control. Now, that never played out.
added_claims.claim: The space-race belief that first to space would control the globe never materialized; the same zero-sum 'whoever controls AGI/ASI controls the globe' belief is likely equally wrong.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: Ideas spread like the wind. They move fast. People study what other people do.
added_claims.claim: Innovation diffuses across firms and countries (OpenAI building on Google, DeepSeek on both), so calling copying theft is selective and prohibiting rivals from AI progress cannot succeed.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: it's really mindboggling to think in n you know in a few short weeks how quickly We went from that level of optimism to this level of concern.
added_claims.claim: CEO sentiment swung from the strongest pro-business optimism in 50 years (Druckenmiller) in January to deep concern within weeks, so sentiment extremes can reverse fast when policy shocks arrive.
added_claims.conditions: Policy shock after an optimism peak.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: Down one day, 4% up the next day, 4% clearly struggling trying to get their hands around uh you know, where we are.
added_claims.claim: Alternating 4% daily moves show that markets cannot price the policy outcome and the 'is it all priced in' question is unanswered.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: There are fears and rumors out there about is our 10-year, you know, do we have demand for it on a global basis? The dollar is is under assault here.
added_claims.claim: Concerns about global demand for Treasuries and a falling dollar added a funding-stress dimension to the tariff drawdown.
added_claims.testable: partly - auction demand and DXY observable

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: I said a few episodes ago the biggest risk on Nvidia was the government. And that turned out to be true here.
added_claims.claim: For a high-flying single stock, government action (export bans, a possible customer audit of shipments to Singapore) is the dominant and least forecastable risk, e.g. $12B of annual China sales at stake.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: He gives two different guides and he says, you know, if there's a recession, which we may have, you know, then earnings are going to be 7 to eight bucks
added_claims.claim: United Airlines gave two guidance scenarios (7-8 dollars EPS if recession, 12 if not); firms withdrawing or widening guidance is evidence of unusual uncertainty that has not yet reached consensus estimates.
added_claims.testable: partly - guidance withdrawal counts can be tracked

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: I think if we're still having this conversation in 8, 12, 16 weeks with this level of uncertainty around tariffs, I think it's going to have a much bigger headwind to those
added_claims.claim: The duration of uncertainty matters: if tariff uncertainty persists 8 to 16 weeks, the hit to S&P earnings grows beyond what a quick resolution would cause.
added_claims.conditions: Condition: no clarity within roughly one earnings season.
added_claims.testable: partly - hard to test with few episodes

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: I asked you should the market be higher or lower from the all-time highs where we started the year, you would say of course it should be lower, right?
added_claims.claim: Given the policy uncertainty introduced since January, a 10% S&P decline is not irrational and does not by itself make the market cheap.

added_claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
added_claims.quote: terms of reference on what the trade deal will be, but it will still take months in order to hammer out
added_claims.claim: Trade-deal frameworks (India: terms of reference only) take months, far longer than the 3 to 4 weeks the president claimed, so uncertainty will outlast the market's patience.

added_claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
added_claims.quote: If we can just get a four-year forecast that it's about reonshoring a few industries, land the plane on China or on on Japan and India
added_claims.claim: Market recovery needs predictability: a credible four-year commitment to narrow reshoring (not Navarro-style replacement of income tax) and concluded deals with China, Japan and India would let companies plan.
added_claims.conditions: Also needs other things to come together.

corrections.fix: Same claim, speaker most likely Bill Gurley.

completeness_estimate: 0.68 - the first reader caught the main policy arguments and market views but skipped historical analogies (Smoot-Hawley, Cold War, space race), data points (Nvidia China share, H20 economics, power build-out) and several supporting mechanisms.
